metadata.title: Kikiria
metadata.description: A game to look, ask and check what you find online.

home.mascotAlt: Roqui, a little detective rooster holding a magnifying glass.
home.title: Can you figure out which one was made with AI?
dialogue: Hi! I’m Roqui, the detective rooster.
Have you ever seen a photo and wondered if it was real?
Computers can now invent photos that look real.
I’ll teach you how to spot them!

briefing: Mission 1! Find the image made with AI.
You will see two images: one is a photo and the other was made by a computer.
Tap the one you think the computer made.
Getting it wrong is fine: that is how we learn.

tutorial.selectedHint: You can change your choice before checking.
tutorial.modelAria: Thinking steps: Look, Ask and Check
tutorial.singleHint: There is nothing to compare it with. Take your time.
tutorial.uncertainHint: Careful: sometimes the right answer is that looking is not enough to know.
tutorial.uncertainCorrect: Exactly! Looking was not enough here.
tutorial.uncertainMissed: This one could not be known by looking alone.

r1.observation: Seeing someone famous does not make the image real.
r1.remember: Find out where it came from.

r2.question: Being viral does not make it true.
r2.remember: Check who posted the meme and why.

r3.verification: A scene looking possible does not prove it happened.
r3.remember: Look for evidence beyond the image.

r1.observation: Compare how the animal and setting fit together.
r1.remember: A visual clue needs more context.

r2.question: Look at how the animal and objects interact.
r2.remember: Coherence helps, but it is not enough alone.

r3.verification: Check the background, water, and pose together.
r3.remember: AI can look completely normal too.

r1.observation: Check how the sofa, ball, and dog fit together.
r1.remember: The whole scene matters more than one detail.

r2.question: Do the landscape and pose fit together?

r3.verification: Compare the cat with what the mirror shows.
r3.remember: An odd reflection is a clue, not proof.

r1.observation: An unusual animal can be completely real.
r1.remember: Looking unusual alone cannot identify its origin.

r2.question: A striking image is not enough to decide.
r2.remember: Do not decide from appearance alone.

r3.verification: Nature can create incredible scenes too.

r1.observation: Seeing Messi there does not prove that moment happened.

r2.question: Recognizing someone in an image is not enough.
r2.remember: Check whether person, sport, and context fit.

r3.verification: Look at the action and balls across the whole scene.
r3.remember: That mismatch is a clue, not proof.

r1.observation: Check the crowd and the background, not only the main figure.
r1.remember: A detail that does not fit can raise questions, but AI images can look correct too. Check the source.

r2.question: Why would this be shown to you?
r2.remember: An image always comes from someone with a purpose.

r3.verification: Before sharing it, find who published it first.
r3.remember: Sharing without checking is part of the problem too.

r1.observation: Compare frame with frame: count the fingers in each one.
r1.remember: Something that changes for no reason between frames is a clue.

r2.observation: Read the sign in all three frames: does it say the same thing every time?
r2.remember: Text inside a video is usually the first thing to slip.

r3.verification: If a video looks odd, find where it came from before believing it.
r3.remember: A video can look perfect and its origin still be unknown.

r1.observation: With no second video beside it, check the movement is even between frames.
r1.remember: Odd movement is a clue, not proof.

r2.question: What might this video have been made for?
r2.remember: A short video is made to be shared quickly.

r3.verification: Sometimes the frames are not enough: find the whole video and its source.
r3.remember: Letters going wrong is a clue, not proof: you still have to find where the video came from.
r3.observation: Look at the letters: a computer often writes shapes that look like words but say nothing.

round1.observation: Compare the whole scene, not just one detail.
round1.remember: Look for more than one clue before deciding.

round2.question: A visible stamp does not confirm the origin.
round2.remember: Check who posted the image and when.

round3.verification: An everyday scene can also be made with AI.
round3.remember: Check origin and context before deciding.

teacher.title: Classroom guide
teacher.lead: This is how Kikiria works in a classroom. No internet needed, and no phones for the students.
teacher.sessionLead: The timings are a guide: if the discussion gets good, let it run.

welcome.title: Ask before you show
welcome.detail: Have you seen pictures online that looked real and were not? Let them tell you.

play.title: Play the first island
play.detail: Hand the phone to someone and let the rest argue out loud before they tap.

versus.title: Versus in turns
versus.detail: Two volunteers pass the phone. The others may give clues, never the answer.

talk.title: Talk it over
talk.detail: Use the prompts below. Getting it right matters less than explaining why.

close.title: Close with a rule
close.detail: Each child names one thing they will check before believing or sharing something.

teacher.promptsLead: They work even if the class got everything wrong. Doubt is the point.

prompts.one: What was the first thing that made you doubt that image?
prompts.two: Who do you think posted that photo, and what for?
prompts.three: Have you ever shared something without checking? What happened?
prompts.four: When is it fine to say "I do not know if this is real"?

teacher.onlineDescription: A code for your students to join, and a view of where the group struggles. It needs a server, and does not exist yet.
teacher.certificateDescription: Recognition for completing the training. It will arrive once the online classroom works.
teacher.privacyNote: The app never asks for a child's real name, age or school. In this version there are no accounts and nothing is uploaded to any server.
teacher.wayCardsDetail: You are the only one with a device. Each student holds up a sheet and you scan the answers with the camera.
teacher.wayPhonesDetail: If some students do have a phone, share the Kikiria address and each of them plays their own progress.
teacher.cardsHowLead: Start to finish. This is the part nobody guesses on their own.

create.title: You say how many students there are

print.title: You print the sheets
print.detail: In black and white. One sheet per student, nothing to cut.

hand.title: You hand one to each student
hand.detail: The big number on the sheet is their id. No name is needed.

ask.title: You ask a question with two options
ask.detail: Read it aloud or show it on screen: option A and option B.

raise.title: They hold the sheet up, turned
raise.detail: For A, the A stays on top. For B, they turn the sheet upside down.

read.title: You scan with the camera
read.detail: Walk around the room and Kikiria notes who answered what, and who is missing.

briefing: You'll see two pictures: a computer made one of them.
Tap the one you think the computer made. Getting it wrong is fine.
education.originVsTruth: Careful: something a computer made is not automatically false, and something a person made is not automatically trustworthy. Always look at the evidence.
education.visualClue: A visual detail may be a clue, but it is not proof on its own: editing, compression, or ordinary mistakes can cause odd details too.
education.sourceQuestion: Who published this, and is the original source available? Compare it with reliable sources.
education.evidenceCheck: Is the image in its original context, and is there enough evidence to decide?
education.remember: In this exercise the origin is known. Outside the game, a clue alone does not prove where content came from.

decisions.decisions1: AIGO isn't hiding any more. Now he floods the feed with messages, and every one of them looks real.
decisions.decisions2: Roqui looks. He looks again. And for the first time, looking is not enough.
decisions.decisions3: "Pass it on," says AIGO. "Everyone else is. What's the worst that could happen?"
decisions.decisions4: Roqui doesn't move. He knows something AIGO doesn't: nobody can make you share.
decisions.decisions4Ask: This is no longer about what it is. It's about what you do.

decisions.title: So what do I do now?

noClass.situation: A message arrives: “URGENT! No school tomorrow”. It was posted by @real_school_news, an account you do not know.
noClass.question: What do you do before changing your plans?
noClass.whyOfficial: The school decides whether there is school. A name can sound official without being it; the answer is born there.
noClass.remember: When something affects you, look for whoever decides it, not whoever repeats it.
noClass.crowd: Believe it, because plenty of people shared it
noClass.whyCrowd: Lots of people repeating it does not confirm it: nearly all of them are forwarding it unchecked too.
noClass.askGroup: Ask in the group whether anyone else saw it
noClass.whyAskGroup: Others having seen it only confirms it is going around, not that it is true.

animalFound.situation: You see a photo of an extraordinary animal with thousands of likes.
animalFound.question: What do you do to find out whether that animal exists?
animalFound.likes: Go by the thousands of likes
animalFound.whyLikes: Being shared a lot does not make it true. Sometimes it is shared precisely because it is surprising.
animalFound.original: Look for where that photo first appeared
animalFound.whyOriginal: The origin tells you who made it and when. That is where the doubt gets settled.
animalFound.friend: Ask a friend whether he thinks it is real
animalFound.whyFriend: Your friend can mean well and still be repeating something they never checked.
animalFound.remember: How many people share something says nothing about whether it is true.

noSource.situation: A striking image is going around with no word of who took it or where.
noSource.question: What do you do with it?
noSource.believe: Believe it, because it looks so real
noSource.whyBelieve: Looking real is not proof. There are computer-made images that look perfect.
noSource.reject: Call it fake, because it has no source
noSource.whyReject: You cannot claim that either. No source means you do not know, not that it is a lie.
noSource.wait: Say it cannot be known yet
noSource.whyWait: That is the honest answer: with no origin there is nothing to check it against, either way.
noSource.remember: “I do not know yet” is a clever answer, not a defeat.

funnyMeme.situation: A meme makes you laugh and you want to send it to the class group.
funnyMeme.question: What do you do first?
funnyMeme.whySendNow: If it turns out to be false, you are the one who spread it. Catching up with it afterwards is very hard.
funnyMeme.checkFirst: Look at where it came from before sending it
funnyMeme.whyCheckFirst: A few seconds before sharing are worth more than a thousand explanations after.
funnyMeme.whyDeleteIt: You do not have to delete everything that makes you laugh. Checking before you pass it on is enough.
funnyMeme.remember: Sharing is publishing too: whatever you forward carries your name on it.

classmateVideo.situation: A video reaches you where a classmate seems to be doing something embarrassing. It looks odd.
classmateVideo.question: What do you do?
classmateVideo.forward: Forward it to ask whether it is true
classmateVideo.whyForward: Asking that way spreads it further. Even if it is false, the harm to your classmate is already done.
classmateVideo.tellAdult: Do not forward it, and tell an adult you trust
classmateVideo.whyTellAdult: You break the chain and you ask for help. An adult can do things you cannot do alone.
classmateVideo.whyIgnore: Not forwarding it is right, but your classmate is still alone with the problem.
classmateVideo.remember: When something could hurt a person, the first job is not to find out: it is not to spread it.

trustedFriend.situation: Your best friend shares a news story that sounds exaggerated to you.
trustedFriend.question: What do you do?
trustedFriend.trustFriend: Believe it, because they are your friend
trustedFriend.whyTrustFriend: Trusting a person is not the same as trusting the information they forwarded.
trustedFriend.askOrigin: Ask them where they got it
trustedFriend.whyAskOrigin: Asking is not doubting them. It is the kind way of checking together.
trustedFriend.argue: Tell them in front of everyone that it is a lie
trustedFriend.whyArgue: You might be right and still humiliate them. And you have not checked it yet.
trustedFriend.remember: People you trust can be wrong without meaning to.

poster.situation: You made a beautiful poster for your school using an AI tool.
poster.question: How do you publish it?
poster.whyAsPhoto: It is not true, and whoever sees it will believe something that never happened. That is the very thing you learned to spot.
poster.whySaySo: It is still yours and still beautiful. Saying so takes nothing away: it adds trust.
poster.remember: Using AI is not wrong. Hiding that you used it is.

sponsored.situation: Your favourite streamer says a game is AMAZING and everyone should buy it. Underneath, in tiny letters: “Ad”.
sponsored.question: What is worth thinking about before you want it?
sponsored.trustHim: “If he says so, it must be the best”
sponsored.whyTrustHim: Liking someone does not make their message neutral. He is still a person, not proof.
sponsored.askWhoPays: “Is he being paid to convince me?”
sponsored.whyAskWhoPays: That tiny word says it: he was paid to talk about it. He may like it anyway, but now you know what is behind it.
sponsored.countLikes: “It has loads of likes, it must be good”
sponsored.whyCountLikes: Likes measure how many people saw it, not whether the game is any good.
sponsored.remember: Before believing someone, ask what they gain if you are convinced.

giveaway.situation: An account promises a new phone: “share this to enter”. Hundreds have shared it already.
giveaway.question: What do you do?
giveaway.shareFast: Share it fast, before it ends
giveaway.whyShareFast: The rush is part of the trick: if they will not give you time to think, it is because thinking would make you doubt.
giveaway.askWhoRuns: Find out who is running it, and whether they exist
giveaway.whyAskWhoRuns: A real giveaway has an owner with a name and rules. If you cannot find them, there is no giveaway.
giveaway.whySendData: Never trade your details for a prize. Very often your details were the prize, but for them.
giveaway.remember: When something rushes you so you will not think, that is exactly when thinking pays.

honest.situation: A creator you like shows some trainers and says straight out: “I was paid for this video, and I do love them”.
honest.question: What do you make of that?
honest.whyIgnoreAll: Being paid does not make her a liar. Distrusting everybody is not thinking: it is giving up.
honest.listenKnowing: Listen to her, knowing it is an ad
honest.whyListenKnowing: She told you what was behind it. Now you get to decide, which is exactly what you wanted.
honest.buyAnyway: Buy them because she has them
honest.whyBuyAnyway: That they suit her says nothing about whether you need them.
honest.remember: Someone saying “this is an ad” is a good sign: they are giving you what you need to decide.

chocolate.situation: You ask an AI whether you can give your dog chocolate. It answers, very sure: “a little won't hurt”.
chocolate.question: What do you do?
chocolate.whyObeyIt: Sounding sure and being right are not the same. Here it was wrong: chocolate really does harm dogs.
chocolate.askAgain: Ask it again until it says what I want
chocolate.whyAskAgain: Asking a hundred times does not change the truth. It only changes the answer until you like it.
chocolate.checkFirst: Do nothing yet and check with someone who knows
chocolate.whyCheckFirst: A vet, a grown-up, a veterinary site. Chocolate is toxic to dogs, and waiting costs nothing.
chocolate.remember: When a decision could hurt someone, check before you act.

homework.situation: You asked an AI to explain a topic for your homework, and it answered very confidently.
homework.question: What do you do with that answer?
homework.whyCopyIt: Sounding sure is not the same as being right: these tools get things wrong without warning.
homework.checkAndCredit: Check it in another source and say you used it
homework.whyCheckAndCredit: That way it is help rather than an oracle, and your teacher knows how you worked.
homework.hideIt: Use it and not mention it
homework.whyHideIt: Even when it is right, you are presenting as yours work you did with help.
homework.remember: An answer that sounds convincing still needs somebody to check it.

admits.situation: You ask an AI something hard and it replies: “I'm not sure, better check it here”.
admits.question: What do you make of that answer?
admits.whyUselessTool: The opposite: saying “I don't know” is the most useful thing a tool can do when it does not know.
admits.goodSign: That it is a good sign, and I will check it
admits.whyGoodSign: Prefer one that admits doubt over one that invents with confidence. The second leaves you worse off.
admits.keepAsking: Ask a different one until I get a confident answer
admits.whyKeepAsking: You would search until you found the one that sounds surest, which is not the one that knows most.
admits.remember: “I'm not sure” is not a failure. It is information.

briefing: This island is unlike the others: you will not be looking at a single photo here.
I am going to tell you things that could really happen. A message, a video, a friend.
And you choose what you would do. Nothing to guess: something to decide.
decisions.briefingAria: Message {current} of {total}. Tap to see the next one.

finale.title: You finished the map!
finale.line: You do not need anyone to tell you where to look any more. Now you know what to ask.
